title: Staff Appreciation That Is Not Jeans Day, Rated
author: RatedEd
summary: RatedEd compares what common staff-appreciation gestures cost per person with what teachers report valuing, and finds the highest-value moves are mostly free. Covering a colleague's duty period, writing a specific handwritten note, cancelling a Friday meeting, offering choice in professional learning and bringing unannounced food all rate five or four stars, while branded swag and a paid jeans day rate poorly. The post is explicit that appreciation does not replace pay, workload or staffing, and frames its advice for principals who cannot fix pay this month but can change Thursday. It argues that what is scarce in a school is time, autonomy and attention, so those are the things worth giving. It closes with a plan for a $500 budget and sixty staff that avoids dividing the money into small gifts.
points: Four of the five highest-value appreciation moves cost nothing, because teachers value time, autonomy and attention more than objects.
Covering a teacher's duty period earns the top rating because it returns twenty-five uninterrupted minutes, and it works best delivered without ceremony.
A handwritten note only counts when it names what the leader saw, on what day, with which student, since specificity is proof of attention.
Scheduled events and swag underperform: a catered lunch often consumes the very break it celebrates, and branded items read as marketing wearing appreciation's clothes.
With a small budget, do not divide it into small per-person gifts; spend it on unannounced food, recurring duty coverage and the thing staff have already asked for.
quotes: The gap between those columns is the entire post, and it goes in a direction that should make budget conversations easier rather than harder. The highest-value moves on this list are mostly free.
Time is the scarcest thing in the building and everyone knows it. Twenty-five minutes back is real, it is immediately usable, and it signals that leadership understands what the day actually costs.
Specificity is proof of attention, and attention is the thing being asked for. “Thanks for all you do” says nothing and everyone knows it.
The unannounced part is the active ingredient. A scheduled appreciation event is a thing on the calendar. Food that appears on a hard day is someone paying attention to the day.
It usually consumes the lunch period it is meant to celebrate, which means the appreciation event takes away the twenty-five minutes we just established is the most valuable thing you have.
Most of it does not. It goes in a drawer, and everyone is polite about it, which is why leaders keep buying it.

A jeans day is a temporary suspension of a rule. Framing the removal of a restriction as a gift tells staff exactly how the restriction is understood by leadership, which is as something they are being permitted rather than something with a reason.
What is scarce in a school is time, autonomy, and attention. Those are the things worth giving.
